claims.tx: Aristotle's central task in De Anima is to answer "What is the soul (psychē), and what does it do?"

Knowledge of the soul "contributes greatly to the advance of truth in general, and, above all, to our understanding of Nature, for the soul is in some sense the principle of animal life" (DA I, 402a5-7).

In De Anima Aristotle seeks to define the essence of the soul, analyze its faculties (nutritive, sensitive, appetitive, locomotive, imaginative, intellective), explain how the soul relates to the body, and understand perception, imagination, and thought.
Aristotle rejects Plato's dualism: the soul is not a separate immaterial entity, but the form or organizing principle that gives the body its life-function.

It is in De Anima that Aristotle most clearly engages the relationship between the soul and the senses, and demonstrates how phantasia plays an integral role in psychic processes — perception, cognition, deliberation, interpretation.

iCit.l: DA III.3, 428a1-3
iCit.r: Phantasia faculty definition is the proximate canonical anchor.

claims.tx: The question of phantasia — what it is, how it functions, and why Aristotle accords it a pivotal role — is among the most crucial elements underpinning Aristotle's psychology, and perhaps the most challenging to pin down.
claims.fr: User-voice framing claim ('perhaps one of the most challenging to pin down'); appropriately hedged.

claims.tx: Phantasia resists simple translation; it occupies a structural position between direct sensation (aisthēsis) and thought (noesis), between the body's reception of sensible forms and the soul's capacity to deliberate, judge, act, and feel.

sCit.l: Hawhee, Aristotle's Eyes p.141 (semantic breadth note)

claims.tx: Per Frede, phantasia designates capacity, activity-or-process, and product-or-result; "appearance in a wider sense" is the central meaning to which all three relate.
Aristotle defines phantasia as "that in virtue of which an image arises for us," a faculty/disposition "in virtue of which we discriminate and are either in error or not" (DA III, 428a1-3).
Phantasia is fundamental for thinking: "To the thinking soul images serve as if they were contents of perception... That is why the soul never thinks without an image" (DA III, 431a15-17).

"Sometimes by means of the images or thoughts which are within the soul, just as if it were seeing, [the soul] calculates and deliberates what is to come by reference to what is present" (DA III, 431b6-8).

Mental calculation, per O'Gorman, "consists of 'combination' (sumplokē) and is essential to the formation of opinion (doxa) through practical reasoning and the realization of truth (alēthēs) through contemplative thought" (O'Gorman, p. 20).
Phantasia functions to mediate sense perception and deliberative or speculative thinking; it "ties abstract thought to concrete perceptible objects or situations" (Nussbaum 265).

claims.tx: Phantasia is fundamental to human thought and mental operations, but is not among "things that are never in error: e.g. knowledge of intelligence; for imagination may be false" (DA 428a16-18).
Phantasia is active when we see a hazy figure in the distance and determine it to be a man, only to find as we approach that it is a small tree.
claims.fr: Classic Aristotelian example; the soft flag is the use of 'In this sense' at the head of the sentence — acceptable.

claims.tx: All images brought to the mind by phantasia have their origin in direct sense perception (aisthēsis); phantasia is causally related to perception — "imagination must be a movement resulting from an actual exercise of a power of sense" (DA III, 429a2).

Phantasia is activated "when there is some failure of accuracy in [direct sensation's] exercise" (DA 428a14-15); it supplies what is missing when the object cannot be perceived or is not definitively perceptible.
Although phantasia is a distinct capacity, it "is not found without sensation, or judgment without it" (DA 427b15).
White interprets phantasia as an intermediary between sensation and thought (nous), facilitating the transition from immediate sensory reception to abstract reasoning and deliberation.

Phantasia is a movement resulting from actual sensation, persisting after the sensory experience ceases; this persistence allows for the retention and manipulation of phantasmata, essential for memory, imagination, and deliberation.

claims.tx: There are four distinct temporal events involved in phantasia's operations: T_1 (original sensory encounter), T_2 (perceptual actualization — the soul undergoes kinēsis being affected in the act of perception), T_3 (creation of resonant motion — a kind of inner likeness, a resonant motion, is generated and remains in the soul; not memory but a re-presenting), T_4 (activation of the phantasma — phantasia draws upon or reactivates the resonant motion to generate an internal image in recollection, imagination, reasoning, or opinion-formation).

claims.tx: The chapter advances a sustained interpretive reading of Aristotle's account of aisthēsis, phantasia, cognition, and appetitive action as a single architectural sequence: a progressive chain of actualizations through which the journey from sensible object to completed action is depicted as a series of iterated motions linking completed actualities.

claims.tx: The chapter's methodological apparatus comprises five elements: the three-factor kinetic schema; the priority of actuality; the structural principle that each motion is named by its terminus; the scale-invariance of relative unmoved originators; and the interlocking of actuality-first architecture with the iterated chain.

claims.tx: The actualization chain organizes Aristotle's analyses of perception and action into FIVE principal nodes: A_0 (motion and time as the first actuality), A_1 (the preconditions under which perception can occur), A_2 (completed perception together with the dual residual trace it deposits), A_3 (the phantasma proper, generated from the resonant kinēsis at A_2), and A_4 (the completed cognitive actuality produced when the rational cognitive apparatus engages the phantasma).

claims.tx: Aristotle supplies the components for the chain: the three-factor kinetic schema (DA III.10, 433b12-25); the definition of motion (Phys. III.1, 201a10-14); the definition of time (Phys. IV.11, 219b1-2); the priority-of-actuality doctrine (Met. IX.8, 1049b12-1050a16); the hylomorphic account of perception (DA II.12, 424a17-24); the treatment of residual motion (On Dreams 2, 459a24-460b3); the dependence of thought on images (DA III.7 431a15-17; III.8 432a3-9); the enmattered-accounts framework (DA I.1, 403a25-b19); and the practical syllogism (MA 7, 701a7-35).

claims.tx: Phantasia ontologically depends on aisthēsis (direct sense-perception) in an asymmetrical relationship; it is, as Aristotle states, "impossible without sensation" (DA III.3, 428b11-12).

Before analyzing phantasia, the chapter analyzes aisthēsis; before analyzing aisthēsis, the chapter must establish the three ontological components constituting all perceptual events: actuality, motion, and time.
claims.fr: Methodological statement; soft flag adequate.

claims.tx: Actuality is prior in account and substance to potentiality (Met. IX.8, 1049b4-10); the potential is intelligible only through the actuality it is potential for, and each motion takes its name from its terminus, not its starting point (Phys. V.5, 229b25).
Motion is the fulfillment of a potential qua potential (Phys. III.1, 201a10) — the ontological hinge connecting one completed actuality to the next.
Time is the number of motion with respect to before and after (Phys. IV.11, 219b1) — derivative from motion and therefore doubly dependent on actuality.

The chain's structural sequence proceeds chronologically because that is how the ensouled body lives through the event: motion and time are experienced together (Phys. IV.11, 219a4) as the passage from one completed state to the next; but at each node, the completed actuality is what makes the preceding motion — and its temporal measure — intelligible. Read the list forward; understand it backwards.
claims.fr: Methodologically explicit ('the list proceeds in the order of lived experience; but the explanatory priority is the reverse'). Beautiful interpretive transparency.

claims.tx: Aristotle's schema for any motion: "All movement involves three factors, (1) that which originates the movement, (2) that by means of which it originates it, and (3) that which is moved" (DA III.10, 433b12-25).

Aristotle gives us three factors: (1) that which originates movement (to kinoun) — the unmoved originator, i.e., the realizable good (to orekton / to prakton agathon); (2) that by means of which it originates movement (hoi kinei) — the faculty of appetite (orektikon), which 'at once moves and is moved'; (3) that which is moved (to kinoumenon) — the animal, via the bodily instrument (the joint as beginning-and-end).

claims.tx: The schema introduced by Aristotle is specifically for locomotive action; its extension to perceptual, phantastic, and cognitive motion is analogical. At the perceptual level, the moved mover (sense-organ) does not mediate between an unmoved originator and moved body in quite the way orexis does at the locomotive level; rather, the actualization of the sense-organ IS the actualization of the organ's capacity. They are the same even under different descriptions.

claims.tx: Each completed actuality is BOTH a terminus that NAMES the motion preceding it (Phys. V.5, 229b25) AND an unmoved source that INITIATES the motion following it. Motion takes its name from its end; the end, once achieved, becomes the beginning of what comes next.

claims.tx: The chain of motion is NOT a sequence of different KINDS of events but the SAME motion-structure iterated at increasing levels of complexity.

claims.tx: At each stage, the moved mover is both patient and agent (Phys. III.3, 202a21-28) — the hinge that converts one motion into the next.

The sense-faculty is moved by the object and moves the organism. Phantasia is moved by the residual trace and moves the psycho-somatic state at the central organ. The rational cognitive apparatus is moved by the phantasma and moves the soul toward its determinate cognitive completion. Appetite is moved by the phantasma-mediated realizable good and moves the body.

claims.tx: Each transition from one actuality to the next is itself a motion: a further actualization of a capacity that was latent in the preceding stage. A_0 → A_1 is the actualization of the world's natural beings (made possible by motion and time); A_1 → A_2 is the actualization of perception (made possible by the sensible object and sense-organ); A_2 → A_3 is the actualization of the completed cognitive actuality (made possible by the phantasma as object of thought); A_4 → subsequent stages is the actualization of appetitive action (made possible by the completed cognitive actuality that discloses a realizable good).

claims.tx: Each transition is a motion in the energeia ateles sense (Phys. III.1, 201a10-14); each terminus is a completed actuality that becomes the unmoved originator of the next. The chain's primitive unit — actuality grounding the motion that produces the next actuality — iterates at every stage, and its specification at A_0 is what licenses everything downstream.

claims.tx: Kenneth Burke's reading of Aristotle's entelechy provides an interpretive resource for understanding how the chain's iterated architecture licenses itself.

Per Burke, entelechy introduces 'another kind of priority, namely the principle involved in a given form' — a priority that runs opposite to temporal sequence. 'A stage that follows another in time may be prior in form and substantiality: "man is prior to boy because man has already attained its complete form whereas boy has not"' (Grammar 261).

The distinction Burke draws — between temporal priority and priority in form and substantiality — is crucial for the chain's structure. Each actuality in the chain stands in BOTH relations to its neighbors.

claims.tx: A_0 is temporally prior to A_1 (motion and time must be in act before sensible objects and sense-organs can actually exist), but A_1 is formally prior to the specific perceptual motions it will ground, just as the completed form of man is formally prior to the boy who is becoming a man.
claims.fr: Interpretive example; flagged.

claims.tx: The chain is, accordingly, NOT a linear sequence of self-sufficient stages but a NESTED architecture in which each actuality licenses and is licensed by others in a reciprocal relation of temporal and formal priority.
claims.fr: Architectural conclusion; user-voice; flagged.

claims.tx: This reciprocal structure is what makes the chain genuinely ITERATED rather than merely sequential: each node is simultaneously the terminus of what precedes it and the principle of what follows it, and each node's intelligibility depends on both relations at once.
